endorsements.title: California AB 3030 (2024), generative AI in patient communications
endorsements.quote: (C) For audio communications, the disclaimer shall be provided verbally at the start and the end of the interaction.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Where patient-facing content is generated by AI, the use of AI in generating that content should be disclosed or otherwise noted within the content.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: • Synthetic content detection and labeling tools and techniques

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Texas has adopted parallel transparency requirements: SB 1188 mandates that practitioners disclose the use of AI for diagnostic purposes to patients15, while HB 149 (the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act) requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI systems, including in healthcare service contexts16.

endorsements.title: Text-to-Video Generative Artificial Intelligence in Pediatrics: Potential Applications, Ethical Considerations, and Future Directions
endorsements.quote: When AI‐generated videos are used for education or preparation, clinicians should disclose that the content is AI‐generated, explain its limitations, and ensure that information aligns with current clinical standards.

evidence.title: Influence of believed AI involvement on the perception of digital medical advice
evidence.outcome: Perceived reliability and empathy of medical advice
evidence.effect: “AI” and “Human + AI”-labelled advice was evaluated as significantly less reliable and less empathetic compared to “Human”-labelled advice (N = 2,280).
evidence.quote: “AI” and “Human + AI”-labelled advice was evaluated as significantly less reliable and less empathetic compared to “Human”-labelled advice.

evidence.title: Ethics in Patient Preferences for Artificial Intelligence-Drafted Responses to Electronic Messages
evidence.outcome: Patient satisfaction, usefulness, feeling cared for by AI vs human vs no disclosure of message authorship
evidence.effect: AI disclosure lowered satisfaction slightly vs human disclosure (0.13; 95% CI 0.05-0.22) and vs no disclosure (0.09; 95% CI 0.01-0.17); >75% satisfied regardless of disclosure.
evidence.quote: The mean change in score between AI and human disclosure was 0.13 (95% CI, 0.05-0.22) points for satisfaction, favoring human disclosure, and 0.09 (95% CI, 0.01-0.17) points for satisfaction between AI and no disclosure, favoring no disclosure.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence With Youth Codesign to Create Vaping Awareness Advertisements
evidence.outcome: Effect of 'Made with AI' source labels on perceived message effectiveness of health ads
evidence.effect: Labeling showed no significant association with any of 5 PME measures (chi2 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20); sensitivity analysis of the 462 who passed the manipulation check was similar.
evidence.quote: Labeling the ads as AI-generated or created by an official health agency had no significant association with PME among young people.

evidence.title: Patient Perceptions and preferences for the disclosure of artificial intelligence generated draft replies to electronic messages - A qualitative study
evidence.outcome: Patient interpretation of written AI disclosure statements on AI-generated draft replies
evidence.effect: Written disclosure statements did not sufficiently clarify how AI was used; nearly half of participants unable to identify AI as the draft's writer; most still preferred disclosure.
evidence.quote: Patient interpretations of disclosure statements suggested that written disclosure statements did not provide sufficient information to clarify how AI was used, with nearly half of participants unable to identify AI as the draft's writer.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Humanized AI Avatars and Messenger Gender for Dental Postprocedure Instructions: Two Randomized Experiments
evidence.outcome: intention to comply and likelihood of returning to dentist
evidence.effect: AI disclosure did not affect intention to comply (non-significant at 95% CI) but reduced likelihood of returning to same dentist vs real person (P<.01; Cohen d=0.35 disclosed humanized, d=0.37 disclosed animated).
evidence.quote: AI disclosure did not affect intention to comply but reduced the reported likelihood of returning to the same dentist.

evidence.title: Applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Strabismus Surgery Video-Based Education
evidence.outcome: Patient recognition that educational video with clinician avatars was AI-generated
evidence.effect: Patients generally did not recognize the video was AI-generated (4.3 ± 1.1 on Likert scale); they would watch more AI videos (4.7 ± 0.7) and recommend them (4.7 ± 0.65).
evidence.quote: Additionally, patients generally did not recognize that the video was AI-generated (4.3 ± 1.1), responded that they would watch more AI-generated videos in the future (4.7 ± 0.7), and would recommend AI-generated content to others (4.7 ± 0.65).

evidence.title: Rethinking Pediatric Asthma Education Through Large Language Model Generation and Simplification: Randomized Double-Blind Study
evidence.outcome: Participants' ability to identify AI-generated versus human-authored patient education material
evidence.effect: Only 7.3% (25/344) of participants assigned to LLM groups identified the material as LLM-generated, versus 80.6% (141/175) of PEAR participants identifying human authorship; overall correct identification 32%.
evidence.quote: While 80.6% (141/175) of participants in the PEARs group accurately recognized published expert-authored content, merely 7.3% (25/344) in the AI-generated groups correctly identified the content as LLM-generated.

commentary.bottom_line: Five simulated studies suggest that AI labels may slightly lower patient ratings of reliability, satisfaction, or willingness to return without changing intention to follow advice, and one qualitative study found that written labels often did not tell patients that AI wrote the draft. No study tested labeling in live clinical messaging, so whether labels correct patients' assumptions about authorship remains unshown.

perspectives.view: All five tests used simulated or offline settings, and none measured whether labels corrected misattribution in real patient messages. Satisfaction effects were small (0.13 and 0.09 points), a labeled-ad trial of 614 found no effect, and a vignette study of 2,280 found lower reliability and empathy ratings. Indirectness and inconsistency support low certainty.

In one trial 7.3% of participants identified LLM-written material, and in another, patients generally missed that clinician avatars were AI-generated. In the only test of comprehension, nearly half of 30 portal users still could not identify AI as the draft's writer after reading a written disclosure, which suggests label wording may determine whether it works.

No study measured labeling inside a live portal or messaging workflow, so fidelity, placement, and clinician burden are unknown. The qualitative study of 30 portal users suggests that a generic statement attached to a draft reply may be misread, and that label design would need testing with patients before rollout.

None of the five tests reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The one non-English population appears in a hazard study from China, where 32% overall correctly identified authorship. Written disclosures that confused portal users may be harder for low-literacy readers, but no study examined this.

California AB 3030 requires disclaimers, including verbal ones at the start and end of audio interactions, and Texas statutes require AI disclosure in some settings. These mandates rest on transparency principles, and the available study does not show that a compliant written label improves patient understanding of authorship.

Most patients in the qualitative study preferred disclosure even when they could not interpret it, and over 75% of 1,455 respondents were satisfied regardless of disclosure. Disclosure reduced willingness to return to the same dentist (d=0.35 to 0.37), which suggests labels may affect trust while honoring patients' stated wish to know.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested labeling of AI-generated messages in a live patient portal or phone line with a measure of whether patients correctly understand who wrote the message and whether a clinician reviewed it. Trials comparing label wording, placement, and audio formats, with outcomes that include comprehension, trust, and follow-up contact with a human, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the five studies testing labels reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. The only non-English population appears in a hazard study, so the effect of labels for patients who most need plain-language or translated disclosures is unknown.
